strengths: Significance: PODS addresses a useful practical question: whether generating additional candidates while retaining a fixed policy-update budget improves RL training. The framework is simple and potentially easy to integrate into GRPO.

Soundness: Lemma 3.1 provides a useful structural characterization of a maximum-variance subset, yielding an efficient selection algorithm. This supports the computational tractability of the proposed selection rule.

Empirical evidence: Figure 1 shows a consistent accuracy advantage on GSM8K for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at comparable reported training times, reaching approximately 81.8% versus 80.9%. Eight independent training seeds and repeated checkpoint evaluations are welcome.

Presentation and originality: The manuscript clearly separates the framework, selection criterion, and algorithm. Applying reward-variance maximization to within-prompt rollout selection is a concrete methodological contribution, although its broader novelty is not fully established.
weaknesses: Soundness—central justification: The theory establishes how to maximize reward variance, not why doing so improves policy optimization. Reward-dependent selection and recomputing advantages on the selected subset change the update distribution. Their effects on the learning objective are not analyzed. Because selected advantages are standardized, larger raw reward variance does not itself establish more informative gradients; the information-theoretic characterization is unsupported.

Evaluation—missing controls: Section 4 compares only GRPO with 16 rollouts against PODS generating 32 and retaining 16. There is no GRPO baseline using all 32, no evaluation of the proposed max-reward alternative, and no ablation of subset versus full-group advantage normalization or the sampling ratio. The experiment therefore does not establish whether max-variance selection is the best use of additional generation or which component explains the gain.

Significance—efficiency claims exceed evidence: A single-A6000 LoRA experiment cannot establish reduced distributed communication or scalability across hardware environments. No generation/update timing breakdown, peak-memory measurement, throughput analysis, or distributed experiment is supplied. Both evaluated methods update on 16 rollouts, so the comparison does not directly demonstrate reduced update memory. The scope should be narrowed to the observed accuracy-versus-time improvement.

Reproducibility: Several consequential details are absent: the exact correctness/format reward and weights, prompt template, training and evaluation decoding settings, prompt batch size, gradient accumulation, clipping parameter, update schedule, and handling of zero reward variance. No implementation is provided or linked. Zero-variance groups make the stated advantage formula undefined, so the omitted handling is operationally important.

Statistical reporting and breadth: Evaluation covers one model, one dataset, and one sampling configuration. The manuscript does not explain whether standard errors are calculated across eight independent training runs or pooled checkpoint evaluations; repeated evaluations within a run are not independent training replicates. Numerical results and a clear aggregation procedure would make the relatively modest improvement easier to assess.

Originality, limitations, and ethics: The claimed first application of rollout data selection to LLM RL is stronger than the related-work comparison substantiates. The conclusion acknowledges future extensions but does not adequately discuss selection-induced bias, sensitivity to extreme or noisy rewards, or hardware-dependent generation costs. No material ethical concern is apparent in the GSM8K experiment, but the claimed applicability to general RLHF pipelines is not evaluated.

strengths: Significance: Separating the number of generated rollouts from the number used for updates is a practical idea that could improve training under constrained update budgets. PODS is simple and readily implementable.

Soundness: Lemma 3.1 establishes the existence of a variance-maximizing subset drawn from the reward extremes, supporting an efficient selection procedure. This is a useful, albeit limited, theoretical result.

Empirical evidence: Figure 1 shows a roughly one-percentage-point final accuracy advantage on GSM8K at similar elapsed time. Eight training seeds and repeated checkpoint evaluations provide more credible preliminary evidence than a single-run comparison.

Presentation: The manuscript clearly describes the framework, objectives, and selection algorithm. Several training hyperparameters are supplied. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent in the benchmark fine-tuning setting.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theory establishes how to maximize reward variance, not why doing so improves policy optimization. Rewards are subsequently standardized within the selected subset, and reward-dependent selection changes the update distribution without a selection correction. Neither analysis nor diagnostics establish when this altered objective produces more informative gradients. Calling the method information-theoretically motivated or the selected subset maximally informative exceeds the demonstrated result.

Evaluation: Section 4 tests only Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with LoRA on GSM8K, comparing GRPO with 16 rollouts against PODS generating 32 and selecting 16. There is no GRPO-32 baseline, measured random-selection control, max-reward ablation, or rollout-ratio sweep. Although random selection is distributionally equivalent to GRPO-16, its timing would differ. These missing comparisons prevent assessing whether max-variance selection offers the best tradeoff or improves over simpler filtering strategies.

Efficiency claims: Figure 1 reports elapsed time on one A6000, but the paper supplies no generation/update timing breakdown, peak-memory measurements, throughput results, or distributed experiments. Both tested methods update on 16 rollouts, so the comparison does not directly demonstrate reduced update memory or communication. Claims about resolving distributed synchronization bottlenecks and applicability at any scale remain unsupported.

Reproducibility: The manuscript does not provide code or specify the exact correctness/format reward, prompt template, training and evaluation sampling parameters, prompt batch size, gradient accumulation, clipping threshold, update schedule, or inference implementation. Handling zero reward variance is also unspecified despite division by the subset standard deviation. These details materially affect both learning and wall-clock results.

Statistical reporting: Section 4 describes eight training seeds and five evaluations per checkpoint, but does not explain how these nested repetitions enter the reported standard errors. Figure 1 therefore leaves uncertainty about whether its intervals correctly reflect variation across independently trained models. Numerical results and a precise definition of the timed workload would strengthen the comparison.

Originality and limitations: The specific application of reward-based subset selection to GRPO has merit, but the conceptual advance over established data selection and prioritized replay is modest, and the claimed first application is insufficiently substantiated. The conclusion acknowledges future datasets and algorithms but does not adequately delimit the current evidence or discuss selection bias, reward outliers, and homogeneous-reward groups. The useful preliminary result is insufficient to support the paper's broad methodological and systems claims.

strengths: Significance: PODS addresses a useful practical question: whether generating more rollouts than are used for updates improves training under resource constraints. The framework is simple and could be readily integrated into GRPO implementations.

Technical contribution and originality: Lemma 3.1 establishes that an optimal reward-variance subset can be formed from the lowest and highest rewards, enabling efficient selection instead of combinatorial enumeration. This gives the proposed heuristic a concrete algorithmic foundation.

Empirical evidence: Figure 1 shows a promising accuracy-versus-wall-clock improvement on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, reaching approximately 81.8% versus 80.9%. Eight independent training seeds and repeated checkpoint evaluations are valuable features of the evaluation.
Presentation: The manuscript is concise, and the framework, selection objective, and training configuration are generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central rationale: The theory establishes how to maximize reward variance, not that this maximizes learning information or improves policy optimization. Advantages are renormalized within the selected subset, so larger raw reward variance does not directly imply stronger or better gradients. Reward-dependent selection also changes the update distribution; the manuscript does not characterize its implications. Calling the selected subset 'maximally informative' therefore exceeds the theoretical evidence.

Experimental isolation: Section 4 compares only GRPO with 16 rollouts against PODS generating 32 and retaining 16. This supports the combined intervention in one setting but does not establish the specific value of max-variance selection. Missing comparisons include training on all 32 rollouts under matched time, alternative selection rules such as the introduced max-reward strategy, and different selection ratios. These are needed to understand whether the gain justifies discarding rollouts and which component produces it.

Efficiency claims: The manuscript claims reduced memory and communication costs and applicability to distributed training at any scale, but reports only accuracy versus time on one A6000. There are no peak-memory measurements, generation/update timing breakdowns, or distributed experiments. Both evaluated methods update on 16 rollouts, so the comparison does not directly demonstrate reduced update costs relative to the tested baseline.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting: Several consequential details are missing, including the exact correctness/format reward formula and weights, prompt template, sampling and evaluation decoding settings, prompt batch size, update schedule, clipping parameter, and handling of zero reward variance. The manuscript also does not explain how standard errors combine eight training seeds with five evaluations per checkpoint, or precisely what the timing includes. No implementation or complete configuration is supplied.

Significance, originality, and limitations: The empirical evidence is restricted to one model, one dataset, one hardware configuration, and one rollout ratio. The novelty is primarily a simple selection rule within GRPO; the manuscript does not yet establish broader empirical utility or new understanding sufficient to support its sweeping conclusions. Future extensions are acknowledged, but failure modes involving tied rewards, noisy reward extremes, or selection-induced distortions are not examined. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the decisive concerns are evidential support and reproducibility.

strengths: Significance: Decoupling rollout generation from policy-update batch size addresses a practical resource-allocation problem in LLM reinforcement learning. PODS is simple and potentially useful when training memory limits the number of rollouts that can be updated.

Technical soundness: The extreme-reward subset argument and prefix-sum implementation support the claimed O(n log n) solution to reward-variance maximization. The binary-reward specialization provides a particularly straightforward selection rule.

Empirical merits: Figure 2 shows promising accuracy improvements under equal wall-clock budgets on GSM8K and MATH, with both single-GPU LoRA and multi-GPU full-parameter training. The rollout-size, update-size, and selection-rule ablations provide useful initial evidence.

Presentation and originality: The framework, objectives, and pseudocode are easy to follow. Applying within-prompt reward-diversity selection between generation and updating is a coherent methodological contribution, even though its ingredients are simple.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion appropriately acknowledges distribution shift, limited task coverage, and prompt diversity as an alternative allocation strategy. The broader-impact discussion recognizes potential misuse; no material ethical concern is apparent from the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness of the experimental comparison: Section 4.1 does not fully isolate the effect of informative selection. Single-GPU comparisons change generation count while keeping update size fixed. The multi-GPU comparison changes rollout group size from 32 to 128 and accumulation steps from 16 to 4, affecting advantage normalization and potentially prompt composition. Gradient accumulation alone does not imply repeated sampling of the same prompt, so the claimed 512 rollouts per prompt requires an explicit sampling schedule. Matched-generation comparisons with full updates and random selection, together with controlled prompt counts and optimizer schedules, are needed.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate. Section 4 leaves the promised code location blank. The manuscript omits the number of independent runs, seeds, the sampling unit underlying the reported standard errors, decoding settings, precise reward definitions and weights, and several batching and evaluation details. Consequently, the modest accuracy differences and their uncertainty cannot be reliably assessed or reproduced.

The systems claims exceed the measurements. No generation/update timing breakdown, peak-memory measurement, communication profile, or utilization evidence substantiates the claimed computational bottleneck and its mitigation. Figure 2 actually shows higher per-step time for PODS on the single-GPU setups, approximately 10 versus 8 seconds. This is compatible with better accuracy per unit time, but does not establish reduced end-to-end step cost. The multi-GPU speedup also needs separation from the simultaneous batching changes.

The theoretical result establishes optimality for a reward-variance surrogate, not preservation of useful policy gradients or improved learning. Advantages are restandardized on the selected subset, and reward-dependent selection changes the sampling distribution without selection-probability correction. The manuscript honestly acknowledges this bias, but its stronger claims of cleaner learning signals and harmful additional samples remain unsupported. Diagnostics of gradient quality, zero-advantage groups, or prompt reweighting would help establish the proposed mechanism.

The evidence supports a narrower contribution than the stated generality. All experiments use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and selection-rule ablations cover only GSM8K with single-GPU LoRA. Figure 2(c) primarily shows faster learning, with similar final accuracies, rather than compelling evidence of superior convergence. A tuned baseline allocating resources to more distinct prompts, and a comparison with zero-variance-group filtering, would clarify the practical advantage over nearby strategies.

Important implementation cases are undefined: the advantage formula divides by zero when selected rewards are identical, and tie-breaking is unspecified despite extensive ties under binary rewards. In addition, experiments combine correctness and formatting rewards without explaining whether the general variance-maximization algorithm or the binary shortcut is used. These choices directly affect both the learning signal and reproducibility.

strengths: Significance: Decoupling rollout generation from policy-update volume addresses a useful practical problem. PODS is simple to integrate into GRPO and could benefit settings where updates are relatively expensive.

Soundness: The extreme-reward subset characterization supports an exact O(n log n) variance-maximization algorithm using sorting and prefix sums. The binary-reward specialization gives an intuitive, inexpensive selection rule.

Evaluation: Figure 2 reports accuracy against actual training time on GSM8K and MATH, covering both single-GPU LoRA and eight-GPU full-parameter training. The distributed experiment shows approximately a twofold reduction in global-step time and faster attainment of high accuracy. Ablations examine rollout counts, update counts, and selection rules.

Presentation and ethics: The method and algorithms are clearly organized. The limitations explicitly acknowledge selection-induced distribution shift and the alternative of increasing prompt diversity. The broader-impact discussion recognizes potential misuse; no material ethical concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theory establishes optimality for reward variance, not preservation of useful policy gradients, reduced gradient noise, or improved convergence. Advantages are renormalized after reward-dependent selection, which changes both the sampling distribution and the update. No analysis or diagnostic connects this change to the claimed 'cleaner learning signal.' The combinatorial theorem therefore does not substantiate the central learning-mechanism claims.

Experimental controls: Section 4.1 changes generation counts in the single-GPU comparisons and changes both generation group size and gradient accumulation in the distributed comparison. Matching 512 generated rollouts alone does not isolate selection from group normalization, prompt allocation, or effective update-batch changes. The manuscript needs explicit prompt-reuse accounting and matched controls, particularly random selection in the distributed setting and a baseline allocating generation capacity to more prompts. The latter limitation is honestly acknowledged, but remains an important unresolved comparison.

Reproducibility: Section 4 leaves the promised code URL blank. It omits the number of independent runs and seeds, decoding settings, evaluation sampling protocol, precise reward components and weights, and handling of zero reward variance. Figures report 1.96 times the standard error without identifying the replication unit or sample count. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of the relatively small final-accuracy gains.

Systems evidence: The claimed memory, communication, and hardware-utilization benefits are not directly measured. There is no peak-memory measurement, utilization profile, or inference/update timing breakdown. Figure 2 actually shows longer single-GPU steps for PODS, approximately 10 seconds versus 7–8 seconds for GRPO; the observed benefit there concerns accuracy per wall-clock budget rather than lower total step cost. The distributed speedup is promising, but its cause is insufficiently characterized.

Significance and originality: The contribution is a useful selective-training heuristic, but the evidence covers only one 3B model and two mathematics datasets, with selection ablations restricted to GSM8K on one GPU. Comparisons with related selective-sampling approaches are conceptual only. This supports a narrower contribution than the claims of an algorithm-agnostic solution and the first principled rollout down-sampling approach.

Presentation and claim calibration: Finite-budget curves do not establish convergence or consistently higher asymptotic accuracy; the distributed curves finish close together. The description of the displayed PPO-style clipping objective as allowing substantially greater probability reductions for negative examples is also misleading: its clipped surrogate limits incentives in both improvement directions. Overall, the promising empirical results do not overcome the unresolved evidential and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Decoupling rollout generation from policy-update batch size addresses a practical RL training problem. PODS is simple and potentially useful when generating additional candidates is cheaper than training on them.

Soundness of the selection algorithm: Section 3.3 provides a convincing argument that a variance-maximizing subset can be drawn from the reward extremes. The prefix-sum implementation supports the claimed O(n log n) complexity, and the binary-reward specialization is straightforward.

Empirical merits: Figure 2 reports improved accuracy at matched wall-clock budgets on GSM8K and MATH with LoRA, plus faster learning in the eight-H100 full-parameter experiment. Figures 3–4 provide useful ablations over rollout counts, update sizes, and selection rules.

Presentation and originality: The framework, objectives, and algorithms are clearly organized. Applying reward-variance selection between generation and GRPO updates is a concrete methodological contribution, even though selective sampling itself is established.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges its mathematical-reasoning scope, selection-induced distribution shift, and the alternative of increasing prompt diversity. The broader-impact discussion recognizes possible misuse; no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—experimental isolation: The multi-GPU comparison changes both rollout group size (32 versus 128) and gradient accumulation (16 versus 4). Equal total generated rollouts does not isolate selection from changes in advantage estimation, effective update batch size, and update frequency. The claim of 512 rollouts per prompt also requires clarification: gradient accumulation alone does not establish that successive microbatches use the same prompt. Matched-group-size random-selection and smaller-update GRPO controls are needed in this regime.

Reproducibility and statistical support are insufficient. Section 4 leaves the promised code URL blank and does not specify the number of independent runs or the sampling unit underlying the reported standard errors. Training/evaluation decoding settings, exact reward composition and weights, prompt templates, and handling of zero reward variance are also insufficiently documented. Consequently, the reliability of the relatively small final-accuracy gains is difficult to assess.

The central systems explanation is not directly verified. The paper reports total step times but no generation/update breakdown, peak-memory measurements, or utilization and communication measurements. In Figures 2a–b, PODS actually takes longer per step, although it achieves better accuracy over time. The multi-GPU speedup is promising, but the evidence does not establish the broad claims about maximizing inference utilization and reducing communication overhead.

The theory establishes optimal reward variance, not optimal learning signal. It does not show that maximizing reward variance preserves or improves the GRPO gradient, particularly because advantages are renormalized after selection. Selection changes the sampling distribution without a corresponding selection correction. The limitations acknowledge this honestly, but claims that the method removes noise or provides theoretically justified learning improvements exceed the demonstrated result.

Significance and originality remain incompletely established against practical alternatives. All experiments use one 3B model, and selection-rule ablations cover only GSM8K with LoRA. There is no experimental comparison with increasing prompt diversity or filtering zero-advantage groups, despite their direct relevance to the proposed efficiency mechanism. The mathematical characterization is useful but does not by itself establish a substantial advance over simpler balancing/filtering strategies.
Overall, the idea and initial results are promising, but unresolved comparison confounds and missing reproducibility details prevent the evidence from supporting acceptance in its current form.
